etymology: Coined by C. S. Lewis in 1941: the habit of assuming a person is wrong and then explaining, at leisure, why they came to be so wrong.
committed_when: An argument has been made, and its psychology is easier to discuss than its evidence.
tell: The reply explains why you believe it before establishing that it is false. The cause of the belief is offered in place of the truth of it.
counter: Ask for the refutation first and the diagnosis second. A belief can have an unflattering cause and still be correct, so the cause is not the answer.
senses: Refuting an argument by explaining why the person holds it: their class, their income, their resentments, their reading list.
It works because causes are always available and usually unflattering. Any position can be given a psychology, and a psychology is much easier to produce than a counter-argument.
example: *"Of course he thinks the zoning reform is fine - he bought his house in 1998."* The reform is still on the table.

confused_with.tell: Ad hominem attacks the arguer; Bulverism explains the arguer and treats the explanation as the refutation.
